A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ArtVIP and provide readable main text, figures, tables, equations and appendices. Retained material can be matched across the substantial expansion and reorganization.

before.justification: V1 reports original reconstruction and feature-distribution comparisons, measured physical trajectories, real-world imitation-learning results and simulated reinforcement-learning results.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical evaluations and adds microwave transfer comparisons, expanded imitation-learning measurements, computational profiling and generated-asset evaluations.

M1.justification: V3's RL transfer application includes Visual Matching alongside RandomConv, adding a component to the procedure described in v1 (Sec. 5.3). The asset-construction pipeline, joint equations, EAGLE losses and reward remain unchanged. The expanded behavior-primitives description largely documents existing mechanisms.

E1.justification: Beyond the retained four imitation-learning tasks, v3 evaluates door-pulling on an unseen real microwave using simulated microwave instances without an exact digital twin (Sec. 5.2). It also reports real-world CloseTrashcan deployment and evaluates SplArt reconstruction from real cabinet and refrigerator imagery, substantially extending the tested scenarios.

E2.justification: PartNet-Mobility becomes a downstream imitation-learning asset comparator in Table 2, whereas v1 compared it through geometry and appearance. V3 also adds vision-based PPO against EAGLE (Tables 3 and 12) and evaluates reproduced SplArt outputs against ArtVIP assets (Appendix L). ACT and DP remain unchanged comparison methods.

E3.justification: For the original imitation-learning tasks, evaluation changes from 10 rollouts to 60 per training seed, and mixed-data settings expand from 100 real plus 100 simulated trajectories to four simulation-data quantities. New protocols include 500 simulated trajectories per dataset for microwave transfer, simulation and real-world RL trials, and quantitative reconstruction-error evaluation.

E4.justification: V3 adds simulation-data quantity sensitivity experiments and generated-asset failure analysis covering collisions, geometry, joints and materials. It expands v1's profiling discussion into category-wise comparisons of triangle counts, active joints and isolated-object versus kitchen FPS (Table 7). The earlier physical-motion analyses remain present.

E5.justification: V1 provides imitation-learning point estimates without training-seed counts or confidence intervals. V3 specifies three training seeds and reports individual seed scores, means and 90% confidence intervals in Table 10. The existing five-seed RL curve and ten-trial physical evaluations are retained.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces many estimates: ACT PullDrawer success changes from 60% to 64% for real-only training and from 30% to 39% for simulation-only training, under the revised evaluation protocol. New results include DP microwave mixed-data success of 83% with ArtVIP versus 70% with PartNet-Mobility, EAGLE versus PPO checkpoint scores, and FPS and reconstruction-error tables.

T1.justification: The joint-drive, friction, target-position and stiffness equations, together with the learning losses and reward formulation, are retained. Appendix K adds the standard Pearson-correlation formula as evaluation explanation; no substantive theoretical result, assumption, proof or derivation changes.

C1.justification: The central dataset contribution expands from 206 objects across 26 types to 992 objects across 37 subcategories grouped into nine categories. V3 also explicitly claims compatibility through conversion to URDF or MJCF. The principal claims concerning visual realism, physical fidelity and embedded interactions remain.

C2.justification: V3 adds substantive explanations connecting annotation utility to consistent part modeling, FPS behavior to geometry and active joints, and generated-asset failures to camera estimation, training-domain restrictions and rendering incompatibilities. These extend v1's interpretations considerably. The limitation concerning labor-intensive asset creation is retained.

D1.justification: V3 adds an annotation-label catalog, per-subcategory modeling and physics-tuning labor estimates, simulator versions for profiling, and asset-conversion instructions. The abstract replaces the project-page pointer with a direct dataset-hosting link. Existing ACT, DP and EAGLE hyperparameter tables are retained.

R1.justification: The introduction and Appendix L substantially expand positioning against automated articulated-object pipelines, adding discussion of SplArt, Real2Code, Articulate-Anything, ArtGS and ArticulatedGS, among others. V3 develops the argument for manually authored fidelity through specific reconstruction and simulation-readiness limitations, beyond v1's broader criticism of generation methods.

P1.justification: V3 extensively polishes the prose and reorganizes the methodology: production becomes part of Visual Realism, modeling standards move to Appendix D, and Physical Fidelity precedes Modular Interaction. The appendices are reorganized from A.1–A.7 into thematic sections A–M, and the introduction and conclusion are revised.

P2.justification: V3 adds interaction-primitives, microwave-comparison, segmentation and generated-asset figures, substantially expands result tables, and replaces the earlier category chart with a detailed taxonomy table. The overview moves to page 2 and the unchanged RL training curve moves into the appendix. Conference formatting also changes the page layout.

improvement.justification: V3 substantially strengthens v1's limited downstream validation through three-seed imitation-learning evaluation, more rollouts, uncertainty reporting, data-quantity analysis and a direct asset-dataset comparison. Expanded annotation and production documentation also improves usability. A material weakness remains: the claimed RL simulation-to-real correlation cannot be checked because its cited Table 3 contains EAGLE-versus-PPO scores rather than paired simulation and real-world outcomes. Despite that reporting gap, the gains in experimental support and transparency are substantial.
